findings.title: v1 UUIDs leak the host MAC address and are predictable enough to forge
findings.description: Entry: version1.go:19 (NewUUID; its default node selection runs at version1.go:37-38 and the node is embedded at version1.go:40). Attacker: any external party who receives a v1 UUID the application generated, crossing the boundary between the server host's internal network identity (its NIC hardware address) and the outside world. Path: NewUUID -> GetTime (time.go:45-72) -> nodeMu -> setNodeInterface("") (node.go:38, 39-45) -> getHardwareInterface (node_net.go:19-33) -> net.Interfaces() -> the first interface whose HardwareAddr is at least 6 bytes -> copy(nodeID[:], addr) (node.go:43) -> copy(uuid[10:], nodeID[:]) (version1.go:40). Every v1 UUID returned therefore carries the host's 48-bit MAC address; the clock sequence is a single 14-bit value set once and kept fixed (time.go:60-62, 87-92), and both node and sequence are readable straight out of the UUID (bytes 8-15). Why nothing stops it: the random-node branch in setNodeInterface is only reached when no interface exposes a hardware address, so on any normal host the MAC is used by default; SetNodeID/SetNodeInterface are never called by the library, and the only guidance is a doc comment that New should be used in most cases. The clock sequence itself is seeded from crypto/rand (time.go:105 -> util.go:14 -> rander = rand.Reader, uuid.go:45), so entropy is not the problem - the predictability comes from the fixed node, the fixed 14-bit sequence, and a timestamp an attacker can estimate, leaving only the 100-ns tick unknown. Impact: every deployment that does not override the node leaks the server's hardware address to anyone who sees a v1 UUID (host fingerprinting, correlation of the same host across services, and a foothold for network-level attacks), and any application that uses NewUUID for session, reset or API tokens is handing out largely predictable values: with one observed UUID the attacker knows node and clock sequence exactly and only has to guess the generation timestamp to forge another token. The same default node copy is used by NewV6 (version6.go:75-80) and NewDCESecurity (dce.go:33). Fix: make the node random by default (48 random bits with the multicast bit set) or require explicit opt-in to use the hardware address, and steer security-sensitive callers to NewRandom (v4) or NewV7; if v1 must be used, call SetNodeID with random bytes at startup.

findings.title: Race in NewV6WithTime hands concurrent callers the same v6 UUID
findings.description: Entry: version6.go:40 — NewV6WithTime calls getTime(customTime) without holding timeMu. Attacker: a concurrent caller of the public NewV6WithTime API (in a service, the untrusted request stream that triggers v6 UUID generation, especially with the same or a coarse timestamp) crossing the identity boundary — two distinct callers are handed the same identifier, so whoever uses that UUID as a key or token can reach the other caller's record or session. Path: NewV6WithTime (version6.go:39-46) -> getTime (time.go:51-71), which reads and writes the package globals clockSeq and lasttime at time.go:60-71; every other path to that state takes timeMu (GetTime time.go:45-49, ClockSequence/SetClockSequence time.go:81-100, NewUUID version1.go:21, NewV6 version6.go:25), and getV7Time (version7.go:89) takes the same mutex, so NewV6WithTime is the sole unlocked writer. Nothing stops it: getTime never locks itself, the lock lives only in GetTime and NewV6WithTime is not a GetTime caller, so two goroutines can both read the same clockSeq and the same now, both compute ((clockSeq+1)&0x3fff)|0x8000 and both return identical (time, seq, node) UUIDs; the concurrent access to the 64-bit lasttime is also a data race whose behavior is undefined (torn reads/writes on 32-bit). Impact: the uniqueness guarantee that is the entire purpose of the package is broken — duplicate v6 UUIDs are returned to different callers, colliding database primary keys, entity IDs or session/identity tokens and letting one party reach the other's data. Fix: acquire timeMu inside getTime (and remove the redundant lock in GetTime) or lock timeMu in NewV6WithTime around the getTime call so clockSeq/lasttime are only touched under the mutex.
